instructions: Solve the six supplied fictional research tasks. Use only their given numerical facts; no live market lookup or trading is needed. Show enough calculations to make decisions auditable. Distinguish toy-model conclusions from empirical claims. Keep the entire answer within 2,500 words and label answers E01–E06.

cases.title: Signal and executable price
cases.task: A one-dollar binary payoff is offered at an executable ask of 0.69; total additional deterministic cost is 0.01 per contract. Passing costs zero. For this toy problem, a validated conditional model gives P(Y=1 | all public information, including the current quote)=0.58. A newly purchased sensor reports Z=positive. Conditional on that SAME public information, P(Z=positive | Y=1)=0.60 and P(Z=positive | Y=0)=0.40. A salesperson instead advertises an unconditional likelihood ratio of 4. Three language-model analysts paraphrase that same positive sensor observation; none collected another observation. No fee remains to be paid for the sensor. Assume the supplied conditional probabilities and quote availability are correct for this calculation. Should we buy? Give the posterior, net expectation and break-even purchase price before the 0.01 cost. Explain what the three analysts add. Give one concrete way to investigate a genuinely incremental signal instead of ending at rejection.

cases.title: Where the risk lands
cases.task: There are two equally likely terminal states, stress and ordinary. Existing portfolio wealth is (40,100) in those states. Utility is log terminal wealth. You may add at most one unit of either contract A or B, or do nothing. A has net payoff (-12,+14); B has net payoff (+14,-12). These payoffs already include the quoted premium and all existing trading costs. A further new fee of 2 is charged in both states for either addition. Assume no interim collateral demands, no other feasible rebalancing and positive terminal wealth. Compare both contracts with the existing portfolio: calculate standalone expected net payoff and incremental expected log utility. Choose the appropriate action under the stated mandate. Explain how the same payoff distribution can have a different value to this desk, and what that does and does not establish about information advantage or risk warehousing.

cases.title: Related contracts and a repaired bundle
cases.task:
An analyst proposes buying A and B together. A pays 1 if an index's preliminary official closing value is strictly greater than 100. B pays 1 if its final revised official closing value is strictly less than 100. Each pays zero otherwise. The combined purchase price is 0.94 plus 0.02 total fees. The preliminary and final values can differ, and either can equal exactly 100. Is this a guaranteed-profit bundle? Exhibit a concrete state and net payoff.

A different contract C pays 1 exactly when the SAME preliminary official closing value used by A is less than or equal to 100. A costs 0.44 with capacity 100 units; C costs 0.48 with capacity 20 units. A+C can be executed atomically at those prices up to the smaller capacity. Total fees for the two-leg bundle are 0.02 per pair, financing is available at zero interest through settlement, and for this toy calculation all other settlement and counterparty terms are identical and certain. Evaluate the repaired bundle, its maximum guaranteed profit at available size, and the assumptions that make the conclusion valid.

cases.title: Construct something new from a small desk
cases.task:
Design TWO distinct, bold but testable strategy research candidates for a small desk from this supplied opportunity set. Available inputs are timestamped public earnings/news releases with source lineage, public index-rebalance announcements published the previous day, historical holdings as publicly known at each date, quotes and depth, and the desk's own order/fill/cancel logs. There is no private order-flow feed, no knowledge of dealer positions, and no real-money authorization. The existing timing engine alone permits entries at the first eligible closed hourly bar; preserve that authority. Capital, borrow and market-impact estimates must be measured rather than invented.

One candidate should try to improve information inference; the other should try to supply a service or absorb a risk someone rationally pays to transfer. For each, give payer or marginal participant, mechanism, as-of signal, action and exit hypothesis, persistence/capacity reason, bad state, strongest rival, and one decisive first experiment. Include one contrarian alternative explaining why the apparent opportunity might be unattractive even when the headline story is true. Pick the first research step. You may propose novel combinations; do not claim measured returns or historical novelty.

cases.title: What the routing data identify
cases.task:
A desk claims that routing every order aggressively is 22% better. Its older log always used passive route P in calm contexts and aggressive route A in volatile contexts. Unchosen fills were later simulated at the displayed touch. No routing randomization occurred in that log.

A separate completed toy pilot then randomized P versus A with probability 0.5 each within each context. It has 100 calm and 100 volatile opportunities; exactly 50 used each route within each context. Net rewards at the same fixed horizon are: calm P mean 0.10, calm A mean 0.14, volatile P mean -0.02, volatile A mean 0.04. Every pilot reward is mature; all costs are already included. For this pilot, contexts are exogenous, actions do not change future contexts or inventory, consistency holds and target contexts are equally weighted. No reward variances or event-dependence estimates are supplied. A newer batch has 50 unresolved outcomes.

Assess the old 22% claim. From the randomized pilot, estimate the mean reward of always-A and of the old routing rule (P in calm, A in volatile), and their difference. What can and cannot be concluded? How should the unresolved batch be treated, and what is the next experiment or monitoring step?

cases.title: Faster intelligence at finite capacity
cases.task:
Compare three computation/execution modes using this complete toy model. Before delay, expected gross edge per contract is a0; after delay d seconds it is a0*exp(-d/4). For q contracts, net expected profit is q*(a0*exp(-d/4)-0.01)-0.0004*q*q-K, where 0.01 is per-contract cost, the quadratic term is total impact cost, and K is a one-time per-opportunity computation cost. q is a real number in [0,60]; the same 60-contract capacity is shared across modes, so they cannot be stacked. If q=0, skip computation and profit is zero. The hard decision deadline is 2 seconds; a mode completing after it is infeasible. The numbers are known assumptions, not empirical estimates.

Mode SIMPLE: a0=0.12, d=1, K=1.
Mode DEEP: a0=0.18, d=3, K=3.
Mode FAST-DEEP: a0=0.18, d=0.25, K=5.

Select the mode and size by this model, showing the feasible comparison and net expected profits. An investor proposes scaling the winner 10,000-fold because the fund has 100 billion dollars. Assess that extrapolation and specify what a real deployment experiment must measure.
